- **Incidents and maintenance** (`MANAGE_SYSTEM_OPERATIONS`, audited): `POST /v1/status/incidents` with `title`, `components`, `impact` (`minor`, `major`, `critical`, or `maintenance` with `starts_ms` and `ends_ms`) and a first `message`; `POST /v1/status/incidents/<id>/updates` with `phase` (`investigating`, `identified`, `monitoring`, `resolved`; for maintenance `scheduled`, `in_progress`, `completed`) and `message`. An open incident raises its components' state to its impact (minor: degraded, major: partial outage, critical: outage); maintenance does while it runs and is listed ahead of time.

administration.html#storage-credentials-.title: Storage credentials and external locations
administration.html#storage-credentials-.body: Governed lakehouse tables can live on the organisation's own cloud storage, not only in Cairn Store: an Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2 or Blob Storage account (`abfss://`, `wasbs://`), an S3 bucket (`s3://`) or a GCS bucket (`gs://`). Cairn Catalog keeps them like its other tables, Trino and other engines read and write them as the person, and each engine gets short-lived access for the one table it asks for (`/v1/storage`, `cairn.dataaccess.storage_locations`; in the catalog, `catalog/src/external.rs`).

administration.html#streams-kafka-and-ch.title: Streams (Kafka and change data capture)
administration.html#streams-kafka-and-ch.body: A stream writes a Kafka topic into a lakehouse table continuously. Define it with `POST /v1/streams` (`MANAGE_SYSTEM_OPERATIONS`): `name`, `topic`, `format`, `target` (`namespace.table`), and optionally `mode`, `key`, `create_table`, `evolve`, `start` (`earliest` or `latest`), `batch_rows` and `batch_seconds`.

administration.html#synthetic-test-data.title: Synthetic test data

administration.html#table-maintenance.title: Table maintenance
administration.html#table-maintenance.body:
Cairn keeps lakehouse tables healthy with Iceberg's own procedures, run through Trino on a schedule:
- **Compaction** (`optimize`): rewrites files smaller than `optimize_threshold` (default `128MB`) into bigger ones.
- **Snapshot expiry** (`expire_snapshots`): snapshots older than `expire_days`, so the data files only they referenced can go.
- **Orphan cleanup** (`remove_orphan_files`): files no snapshot references, older than `orphan_days`.

- **Policies** (`PUT /maintenance/policies/{scope}`, `MANAGE_SYSTEM_OPERATIONS`). `scope` is `*`, a schema or `schema.table`. The most specific one applies. Each has `optimize`, `optimize_threshold`, `expire_days`, `orphan_days` (null: skip), `every_hours` and `enabled`. Changes are audited (`maintenance.policy_set`).
- **Who runs it.** It runs on a run-as-user Trino connection (`CAIRN_MAINTENANCE_CONNECTION`, a named connection), as the Cairn user `CAIRN_MAINTENANCE_USER` (default `svc-maintenance`). Cairn's policy decides for it as for anyone, so give that user manage on the tables it maintains.
- **When.** The scheduler's leader (`cairn scheduler`) maintains each table whose policy is due. `POST /maintenance/run {"schema", "table"}` runs one now.
- **What happened.** Each operation is recorded with its outcome (`GET /maintenance/runs?table=`). One failing (say, refused) does not stop the next.

administration.html#tokenisation.title: Tokenisation
administration.html#tokenisation.body:
Reversible tokenisation replaces sensitive values with tokens where data lands. The lakehouse then holds only tokens, so every engine, share, export and copy carries only tokens. People allowed to can get the values back from the vault, for a stated purpose, audited.

- **Turning it on.** Set `CAIRN_TOKENS_KEY` to 32 random bytes in base64 (`openssl rand -base64 32`). In Kubernetes, pass it from a Secret through `cairn.extraEnv` (`valueFrom.secretKeyRef`); `CAIRN_TOKENS_KEY_FILE` also works. Without a key, tokenisation is off (503), and values are never kept unencrypted.
- **Token domains.** A domain is a kind of value, such as `email`, `iban` or `patient_id`, with its own random keys. Create one with `POST /governance/tokens/domains` and `{"name": "email", "description": "…"}` (`MANAGE_POLICIES`). The domain's keys are kept wrapped by the master key.
- **Tokens.** A token is `tok_` followed by 26 characters, a keyed HMAC of the value.
  - Within a domain, the same value is always the same token, so joins, counts and group-bys still work.
  - Without the key, nobody can find a value's token by trying candidates, as they could with a plain hash of an e-mail address.
  - Tokenised columns are text.

administration.html#vector-search-on-lak.title: Vector search on lakehouse data
administration.html#vector-search-on-lak.body:
A vector index lets people search a lakehouse table's text by meaning: support articles, tickets, product descriptions, or the text of a files pipe.

- **Define** an index with `POST /v1/vectors` (`MANAGE_INGESTION`): `name`, `source` (`namespace.table`), `key` and `text` (the key and text columns), optional `chunk_chars` (1,500) and `every_minutes`.
- **Embedding.** Cairn splits each row's text into overlapping chunks and embeds them with the deployment's embedding model, the same one search by meaning uses (`CAIRN_EMBEDDINGS`; Ollama in your VPC, or the built-in hashing embedder). The vectors are kept in a lakehouse table of their own, `<source>__<index>_vectors` (key, chunk, text, hash, embedding, model).
- **Kept in step.** Run `POST /v1/vectors/<name>/refresh`, or let the scheduler run it every `every_minutes`. Changed rows are embedded again, new ones added and removed ones dropped. Unchanged rows are not re-embedded; a model change re-embeds everything. Each refresh is one commit.
- **Search.** `GET /v1/vectors/<name>/search?q=...&k=10` returns the closest chunks with their row key, text and cosine score.
  - The caller needs read access to the source table.
  - It is refused when a mask or row filter applies to them there, because the index holds the raw text.
  - Each API replica keeps one index in memory per table version.

administration.html#warehouses-a-trino-p.title: Warehouses: a Trino per team, stopped when idle
administration.html#warehouses-a-trino-p.body:
A warehouse is a Trino of a team's own: its own size, its own queue, its own bill. The same catalogs and Cairn's policies apply. The warehouse proxy (`cairn warehouses`) sits in front, with one port per warehouse.

- **Scale to zero.** After `idleMinutes` without client traffic, the warehouse is stopped. A running query counts as traffic, because its client keeps polling. The next query starts the warehouse, waits until Trino takes queries (`startTimeoutSeconds`, then a short warm-up), and goes through. Queries arriving together share one start. `idleMinutes: 0` keeps a warehouse up.
- **Several nodes, scaled with the load.** Give a warehouse `workers: {min, max, queriesPerWorker, scaleDownMinutes}` and the chart deploys a workers Deployment for it, with the coordinator running no queries itself. The proxy counts the queries running and queued through it, from the statement URLs their clients poll. It keeps `ceil(queries / queriesPerWorker)` workers, between `min` and `max`:
  - more at once when the load rises;
  - fewer after `scaleDownMinutes` of less load;
  - none while the warehouse is stopped.

  A query that arrives with no worker up waits in Trino for one (up to `startTimeoutSeconds`). With Docker, workers are a pool of containers (`"workers": {"docker": {"containers": […]}}`).

administration.html#zero-copy-parquet-fi.title: Zero-copy Parquet: files registered as tables in place
administration.html#zero-copy-parquet-fi.body:
Parquet files already in Cairn Store (written by another system, an export, a Spark job) become an Iceberg table in
Cairn Catalog without being copied. The table then reads the original objects and is governed and queried like any
other lakehouse table.

- **Register** with `POST /v1/lakehouse/parquet-tables` (`MANAGE_INGESTION`): `{"name": "events", "bucket":
  "landing", "prefix": "exports/events/", "target": "files.events", "every_minutes": 60}`. Every `.parquet`
  object under the prefix is taken; names starting with `_` or `.` (`_SUCCESS`, `.crc`) are skipped.
- **Where files may come from.** Only buckets in `CAIRN_PARQUET_BUCKETS` (comma-separated; unset, nothing is
  registered). The person must be able to read the files:
  - a governed volume's bucket (`cairn-vol-<name>`): a read or write grant on the volume;
  - any other bucket: `READ_FILES` on `urn:li:storagePath:<bucket>/<prefix>`, granted by policy like any
    privilege (for example a policy on `urn:li:storagePath:landing/exports/*`). No policy, no read.
- **Schema.** Read from each file's footer (no data is read). All files must have the same columns and types, or
  the registration is refused naming the file that differs. Files written with Iceberg field ids (another table's
  files) are refused.

context-and-ai.html#ai-steward.title: AI steward
context-and-ai.html#ai-steward.body:
Coverage is a catalog's weak point: most tables have no description and no owner, and nobody has time to write ten thousand of them. The AI steward proposes them for people to review.

A run, started from **Semantics › Review queue › AI steward → Find gaps now** or `POST /cairn/api/ai/steward/run`, walks the datasets that lack a description, an owner or a classification, most viewed first. Each proposal carries its evidence and a confidence:

- **Owners.** The people who ran most of the recent queries, who last edited the dataset's metadata, and who own its domain and its upstream tables. Service accounts and Cairn's own automation identities never count, and their queries don't dilute anyone's share. With no clear evidence, nobody is proposed.
- **Classifications.** PII terms for columns, from column names and sampled values. These are the same detectors that label PII during ingestion.
- **Descriptions.** A grounded draft from the schema, lineage and neighbouring documentation, when a model is configured. Drafts count against the AI budget (`max_drafts` per run); when the budget runs out, the run keeps proposing everything else.

**Review.** In the review screen, select many proposals and **Accept** or **Reject** them together. You can edit a description or owner before accepting.

- Each proposal needs the right to make that edit on its dataset (`EDIT_ENTITY_OWNERS`, `EDIT_DATASET_COL_GLOSSARY_TERMS` or `EDIT_ENTITY_DOCS`).
- Accepted owners and terms are written as one bulk batch attributed to the reviewer, so they can be undone like any batch.

context-and-ai.html#assistant.title: Assistant
context-and-ai.html#assistant.body:
Ask questions in plain English from the search bar or the assistant panel. The assistant only uses
metadata you are allowed to see, redacts personal data before anything reaches a model, cites the
assets it used, and can explain lineage anomalies. It runs on Claude or on a local model for
air-gapped installs; without a model it falls back to search-based answers.

context-and-ai.html#context-agents.title: Context agents
context-and-ai.html#context-agents.body:
Context agents read query history, dbt models, BI definitions and pipeline runs and turn them into
**findings** for stewards to review in **Semantics › Review queue › Context findings**:

| Finding | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `METRIC_DEFINITION` | a metric computed the same way in many places, with its definition |
| `DEFINITION_DRIFT` | the same metric name computed differently in two places |
| `TERM_SUGGESTION`, `TERM_LINK` | a missing glossary term, or a term that belongs on an asset |
| `JOIN_RELATIONSHIP` | tables that are routinely joined, and on which keys |
| `DOC_STALENESS` | documentation that no longer matches the data |
| `RUN_ANOMALY` | a pipeline run that behaved unusually |

Accepting a finding writes it to the catalog (glossary terms, relationships, discussions); dismissed
findings do not come back.

**Column lineage from SQL.** On each cycle the agents also read the SQL that writes data: `INSERT … SELECT` and
`CREATE TABLE … AS SELECT` in the query log, and view definitions. Each written column is traced through CTEs,
subqueries, joins, `SELECT *` and expressions to the physical columns it reads, using the catalogued schemas.
The result goes straight into the target's lineage, column by column. A column copied as is is a `COPY`; anything
computed is `SQL`. The statement that produced an edge is kept on it. Cairn only adds what is missing: edges
from crawlers, OpenLineage or people are never removed. SQL that can't be parsed, or tables that aren't in the
catalog, are skipped.

context-and-ai.html#governed-metrics-sem.title: Governed metrics (semantic layer)
context-and-ai.html#governed-metrics-sem.body:
Where teams already define metrics in a semantic layer, Cairn imports them so people and agents query a metric by name instead of writing SQL for it.

**Import.** An administrator posts the file to `POST /cairn/api/context/semantic/import` with `{"format": "metricflow" | "cube" | "lookml", "content": "<file text>", "ref": "<path>"}`. Supported:

- **dbt Semantic Layer (MetricFlow):** simple, ratio and derived metrics over semantic models' measures, with their dimensions and default time dimension.
- **Cube:** each cube's measures (`count`, `sum`, `avg`, `min`, `max`, `count_distinct`, `number`) over its `sql_table`.
- **LookML:** each view's measures over its `sql_table_name`. Measures that reference other fields (`${total}`) are skipped.

Each metric becomes a metric finding in **Semantics › Review queue**, mapped to the catalog dataset for its table. Approving it makes it a governed, versioned definition that keeps its dimensions and time dimension. Nothing is queryable before it is approved.

**Query.** `GET /cairn/api/context/metrics` lists the approved metrics over datasets you may see. `POST /cairn/api/context/metrics/{name}/query` takes `{"dimensions": [...], "filters": [{"dimension", "op", "value"}], "time_grain": "day|week|month|quarter|year", "limit": 200}`. The SQL is compiled from the definition:

- dimensions and filters must be the metric's own;
- filter values are always literals, and the operators are `=`, `!=`, `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=` and `in`;
- an expression with a subquery is refused.

context-and-ai.html#mcp-for-ai-tools.title: MCP for AI tools
context-and-ai.html#mcp-for-ai-tools.body:
Cairn exposes the catalog to AI coding tools over the Model Context Protocol at `/cairn/mcp/mcp`.
Each request carries the user's own access token, so tools see exactly what the user can see.

```bash
claude mcp add --transport http cairn https://<cairn-host>/cairn/mcp/mcp
```

The first time, the tool opens Cairn in your browser. You sign in and choose what it may do (see
**AI agents** in Administration), and it connects with a short-lived token that acts as you. Tools
without OAuth support can still send a personal access token:
`--header "Authorization: Bearer <token>"`.

What a client gets:

- **Tools**, each with a title and structured output. They search, read assets, lineage and impact,
  check quality and access, find definitions and past queries, answer questions with data
  (`ask_data`), and propose documentation for review.
- **Resources** a client can attach as context:
  - `cairn://asset/{urn}`, `cairn://lineage/{urn}` and `cairn://quality/{urn}`, with the urn
    percent-encoded;
  - `cairn://definitions`, the approved metric and join definitions.
- **Prompts** for common jobs, each chaining the right tools: *Document a dataset*, *Review the
  impact of a change*, *Investigate a data quality issue*, *Answer a question with data*.
- **Completion**: typing a few letters of an asset name in a prompt or resource argument suggests
  matching assets you may see.

**The whole API, as tools** (L154). Everything Cairn's API does is reachable over MCP, not only the
catalog tools above:

context-and-ai.html#usage-cost-and-budge.title: Usage, cost and budgets
context-and-ai.html#usage-cost-and-budge.body:
Every model call is recorded with who asked, which feature (`nlq.plan`, `nlq.answer`,
`docgen.draft`, `lineage.explain`, `assistant.chat`), the model, tokens and an estimated cost, and
is written to the audit log under category `ai`.

```
GET /cairn/api/ai/usage?group_by=task|actor|model|provider|day&days=30
GET /cairn/api/ai/usage?mine=true          # anyone: their own usage
```

Seeing everyone's usage needs `MANAGE_SYSTEM_OPERATIONS`. Costs use list prices, including
prompt-cache reads and writes; set `CAIRN_AI_PRICES` (`{"model-prefix": [input, output]}` in USD per
million tokens) for negotiated rates. Self-hosted models cost nothing.

| Setting | Effect when reached |
|---|---|
| `CAIRN_AI_DAILY_BUDGET_USD` | All AI features fall back to search-based answers until the next UTC day |
| `CAIRN_AI_USER_DAILY_TOKENS` | The same, for that one user |

Documentation drafts return `429` instead of falling back, since there is no non-AI draft.

data-quality.html#data-contracts.title: Data contracts
data-quality.html#data-contracts.body:
A contract is a producer's versioned promise about one dataset. It passes or fails as a whole, so consumers can see "the producer broke a promise" rather than "this table broke". A contract can cover:

- **schema:** columns, their types, and which must not be null. Extra columns are allowed unless `allow_extra_columns: false`.
- **freshness:** `max_age_hours`.
- **volume:** `min_rows` and `max_rows`, or `learned: true` for learned thresholds.
- **quality:** named rules, each written like a monitor (`field_metric`, `custom_sql`, `distribution` or `volume`).

```yaml
dataset: urn:li:dataset:(urn:li:dataPlatform:snowflake,analytics.public.orders,PROD)
version: 1.2.0
owner: urn:li:corpGroup:orders-team
schema:
  columns:
    - {name: id, type: integer, required: true}
    - {name: email, type: string}
freshness: {max_age_hours: 24}
quality:
  - {name: email nulls, type: field_metric, config: {field: email, metric: null_pct, max: 5}}
```

How the parts are checked:

- **Schema** is checked against the catalog. Types compare by family: `VARCHAR(255)`, `text` and `STRING` are all strings, and `NUMBER(38,0)` and `bigint` are both integers.
- **Freshness, volume and quality** become monitors that the contract owns. They are created, updated and removed with the contract.
- The contract is **broken** if any part fails, **pending** while a monitor hasn't reported, and **met** otherwise.
- The status shows as a trust badge on the asset and its data products' marketplace cards, and in the asset's **Contract** tab.

data-quality.html#monitor-types.title: Monitor types
data-quality.html#monitor-types.body:
| Type | Checks | Source |
|---|---|---|
| `freshness` | time since the last update | catalog metadata, or SQL with `timestamp_column` |
| `volume` | row count and its change | catalog metadata or SQL |
| `field_metric` | one column metric: `null_pct`, `distinct_pct`, `mean`, `min`, `max`, `stddev`, `avg_length`, `row_count` | catalog or SQL |
| `distribution` | drift of a column's value distribution | SQL |
| `schema` | added, removed and retyped columns | catalog |
| `custom_sql` | any read-only query that returns a number | SQL (write statements are rejected) |

SQL sources run through a named connection that your administrator configures; credentials never
appear in monitor definitions.

getting-started.html#a-guided-start.title: A guided start
getting-started.html#a-guided-start.body:
The first time you open Cairn's home page, it asks what you mostly do here: **Analyst**, **Data engineer**, **Data steward**,
**Admin**, or **Just exploring**. If your profile already names a role, that answer is suggested. Your answer
shapes three things, and you can change it at any time under **Get started** in the sidebar:

* **A checklist.** **Get started** lists a few first tasks for your role, each with a link to where it is done:
  * Analyst: find a dataset, run a query, save it, build a dashboard, ask a question.
  * Data engineer: connect a source, create a pipe or a flow, schedule it, add a quality check.
  * Data steward: review the ontology's proposals, add a glossary term, set an owner, review access requests.
  * Admin: single sign-on, groups, policies, the AI gateway, budgets.

  A step ticks itself when Cairn sees you did it (for example, once you have a saved query), and you can tick any
  step yourself. Your progress is kept in your profile, so it is the same in every browser, in Cairn Desktop and on
  your phone. **Hide** puts the checklist away; it stays under **Get started**. An administrator can turn the
  question and the checklist off for everyone.
* **The sidebar.** A **For you** group at the top holds the pages your role uses most and the ones you pinned. The
  groups your role rarely needs are folded away; **Show everything** brings them back.
* **The command palette** ranks the actions your role uses most first.

getting-started.html#browse-the-catalog.title: Browse the catalog
getting-started.html#browse-the-catalog.body:
**Catalog** lists every asset in Cairn Core: datasets, dashboards, charts, pipelines and their tasks, ML models
and groups, feature tables and containers. The entity types across the top show how many of each there are;
choose one, then narrow by platform, domain, owner, tag or business term on the left, or search. The page's
address keeps the choice, so a view can be shared. Each result opens its asset page.

Flows made in Cairn are in the catalog from their first publish (as pipelines, with their owner); dashboards,
saved queries, workbooks, ML models and feature tables made in Cairn are registered when they are saved.

getting-started.html#creating-and-changi.title: Creating and changing things: forms
getting-started.html#creating-and-changi.body:
The platform hubs (Ingestion, Lakehouse, Compute, Agents, Machine learning, Security & compliance, External sharing,
Usage & cost, Data quality, Alerts & routing and the others) list each area's items in a table. Each concept has one
home; see [Where things are](/docs/administration.html#where-things-are-one-home-per-concept). Creating, editing or running something opens a form:

* **Fields, not JSON.** Each field has a label and help. Lists take a value per entry (press Enter after each);
  schedules show what they mean as you type (`0 2 * * *` reads "Every day at 02:00 UTC"); durations show their unit
  and the same time in larger units; SQL fields complete table and column names.
* **Pickers search Cairn.** Tables, datasets, connections, warehouses, people and groups, secret scopes and secret
  references, git folders, flows and agents are chosen from what Cairn lists for you. When something is not listed,
  type it and choose **Use "…"**; for a person or a group, choose which it is.
* **Secrets stay secret.** A secret's value is typed into a password field, and Cairn never shows it again: an edit
  form leaves it empty, and typing a new value replaces it.
* **Advanced options.** Rarely used fields are under **Advanced options** at the end of the form. It opens by
  itself when one of them has a problem.
* **Raw JSON.** The **Raw JSON** switch at the top of a form shows the request as JSON. Edit it there and switch
  back: the form takes the values, and keys the form doesn't know are kept and sent.

getting-started.html#data-products-and-c.title: Data products and contracts
getting-started.html#data-products-and-c.body:
**Data products** lists every data product with its domain, owners, assets, health and contract. A product's
page has its assets (with the **output ports**, the assets consumers are meant to read), the contracts on its
datasets, its lineage, its service levels, and access: request it, or subscribe to its changes. Owners and
people with the `MANAGE_DATA_PRODUCTS` privilege on the product's domain make and change products here
(**New data product**, **Edit**, **Delete**); they are kept in Cairn Core, so search and the Marketplace show
them at once.

**Contracts** lists every data contract you may see, **passing**, **failing** or **not checked yet**, with
its dataset, version and owner. A contract's page shows its terms (schema, freshness, volume, quality rules)
and whether each holds now; **New contract** and **Publish a new version** use the same form as
`cairn contract publish`.

getting-started.html#find-data.title: Find data
getting-started.html#find-data.body:
* Type in the search bar (`/`), or open the command palette (`⌘K`). Results show trust signals at a glance:
  certification, quality status, PII and freshness.
* Narrow results with facets: type, platform, domain, certification, quality, sensitivity, owner.
  The query and filters live in the URL, so a search can be shared as a link.
* Discover shows what is trending in your domain, your bookmarks, recently viewed assets and the
  featured data products.

getting-started.html#glossary-and-domain.title: Glossary and domains
getting-started.html#glossary-and-domain.body:
**Glossary** shows Cairn Core's business terms in their groups; a term's page has its definition, related
terms, stewards and the assets that use it. **Domains** shows each domain with its owners, subdomains, data
products and assets. Both are read here and changed in Cairn Core (the page links there); terms are added to
assets with bulk edit, and new terms are proposed by the ontology.

getting-started.html#lineage.title: Lineage
getting-started.html#lineage.body:
**Lineage** draws where data comes from and where it goes for any asset you pick: upstream on the left,
downstream on the right, one to three hops away (assets you may not see are left out and counted). For a
dataset it also lists which upstream columns feed each of its columns, when that is recorded.

getting-started.html#understand-an-asset.title: Understand an asset
getting-started.html#understand-an-asset.body:
An asset page has tabs for **Summary** (description, owners, business terms, downstream use),
**Columns** (types, classifications and whether a column is masked for you), **Discussion**,
**Quality**, **Lineage**, **Access** and **History**.

governance.html#consent.title: Consent
governance.html#consent.body:
Some purposes need a person's consent: marketing, for example. When someone withdraws it, their rows leave every
dataset the people working for that purpose query. This applies on Trino and on direct warehouse connections,
in the SQL editor, dashboards, notebooks, reverse ETL syncs and anything else that reads as those people.

- **A purpose that needs consent** (`MANAGE_POLICIES`): its name, the kind of identifier that links a row to a
  person (`email`, `phone`, `customer_id`, or a kind set in `CAIRN_PRIVACY`), its mode, and its members. Members
  are the users, groups and personas who process data for it. The mode is `opt_out`, where rows count unless the
  person withdrew, or `opt_in`, where only the rows of people who said yes count.
- **Records** come from the consent platform or a person, with `MANAGE_POLICIES` or `MANAGE_CONSENT`:
  `POST /records` with `{"subjects": [{"value": "kim@acme.com", "state": "withdrawn"}], "source": "crm"}`. A
  `hash` (SHA-256 of the trimmed, lower-cased identifier) can be sent instead of a value.
- **Identifiers are never stored**, only their hash. The hash is unsalted because each warehouse computes it from
  its own column to match it. The audit log records counts, never identifiers.
- **Which columns count.** In each dataset, the columns classified for that kind of identifier (`PII.Email`…) or
  named like one (`email`, `email_address`…). Rows with no identifier are kept. A dataset with no such column is
  not filtered.

governance.html#policy-decisions.title: Policy decisions
governance.html#policy-decisions.body:
Every access decision in Cairn goes to the **policy decision point**, which combines role-based
rules (who you are) with attribute-based rules (what the data is: domain, tags, classification,
certification) using **deny-overrides**: a single matching deny wins. Decisions are cached briefly
and every decision is written to a tamper-evident audit log (`GET /cairn/api/governance/audit`).

Metadata changes take effect within seconds: when an owner, tag, term, domain, column label or group
membership changes, cached attributes and decisions for that asset or person are dropped at once, and
a changed catalog policy is re-imported immediately (`CAIRN_MCL_INVALIDATION`, on by default).

Two modes:

* **Additive** (default): Cairn's rules can grant access on top of the catalog's native policies.
  Good for a gradual rollout.
* **Authoritative**: Cairn is the only authority and its deny rules are enforced everywhere. Set
  `CAIRN_AUTHZ_MODE=authoritative` and `CAIRN_NATIVE_POLICIES_ENABLED=false`; the catalog's native
  policies are then imported into Cairn and evaluated alongside its own rules.

Masking applies to every read path: the UI, GraphQL and the REST API (`/openapi/v3` entities,
aspects and lists, and `/openapi/v2` timeseries).

integrations.html#extensions.title: Extensions
integrations.html#extensions.body:
An extension adds to Cairn without changing it. It runs as your own service, and Cairn gives it three things:

- **an API token** that can do only what its manifest asks for,
- **events**, delivered as signed webhooks,
- **sections in the workspace**.

Everything an extension may do is declared in one file, `cairn-extension.yaml`:

```yaml
name: incident-log
version: 1.0.0
publisher: Acme Data Platform
description: Recent quality incidents with each asset's trust badges.
permissions: [VIEW_ENTITY_PAGE]                  # the token can do this and nothing else
scope: {attr: resource.domains, op: contains, value: urn:li:domain:finance}   # optional: only these assets
events:
  - url: https://incident-log.acme.internal/events
    types: [quality.incident.raised, contract.broken]                         # empty = every event
ui:
  - label: Incident log
    url: https://incident-log.acme.internal/ui
    placement: workspace                         # or asset: a tab on every asset page, called with ?urn=
```

**Install it** under **Settings → Extensions**, or with `cairn extension install <folder>`. `cairn extension validate <folder>` checks a manifest without installing it, for the extension's own CI.

A first install shows the API token (`cx_…`) and the event signing secret once. Upgrading with a new version keeps both. Rotate them with `cairn extension rotate <name>`. Disabling an extension stops its token, events and sections at once; removing it deletes them. Every change is in the audit log.

integrations.html#notifications.title: Notifications
integrations.html#notifications.body:
Cairn notifies people in the workspace inbox and, per their settings, in Slack, Microsoft Teams or
email. Routes per domain or event type are configured in **Workspace → Workspace settings → Notifications**;
generic webhooks receive the same events as JSON.

| Channel | Setup |
|---|---|
| Slack | install the Cairn Slack app; set `CAIRN_SLACK_BOT_TOKEN` and `CAIRN_SLACK_SIGNING_SECRET` |
| Microsoft Teams | add a Workflows webhook and set `CAIRN_TEAMS_WEBHOOK_URL` or a per-domain route |
| Email | set `CAIRN_SMTP_URL` |
| Webhook | add a route with a URL |
| Kafka | add a route with a topic; set `CAIRN_EVENTS_KAFKA_BOOTSTRAP` (and `CAIRN_EVENTS_KAFKA_SECURITY_PROTOCOL`, `…_SASL_MECHANISM`, `…_SASL_USERNAME`, `…_SASL_PASSWORD` if needed) |
| Amazon EventBridge | add a route with an event bus name or ARN; the notifier uses the AWS credential chain (`AWS_REGION`) |
| Google Cloud Pub/Sub | add a route with `projects/<project>/topics/<topic>`; the notifier uses its Google identity |

What the notifier will and will not call:

* **Slack** messages are checked against Slack's Block Kit limits before they are sent; long titles
  and bodies are shortened rather than rejected by Slack, and mentions in catalog text are escaped
  so a description cannot ping a channel. When Slack rate-limits Cairn for a few seconds the message
  waits; longer limits are retried on the next delivery round. For GovSlack or an egress proxy set
  `CAIRN_SLACK_API_URL`. Replies to button clicks go only to `hooks.slack.com`
  (`CAIRN_SLACK_RESPONSE_HOSTS` adds origins).

marketplace.html#requesting-access.title: Requesting access
marketplace.html#requesting-access.body:
1. Open a product and choose **Request access**. Pick a purpose and, if offered, a duration.
2. Cairn shows what you would get before you submit (`POST /cairn/api/marketplace/access-requests/preview`).
3. The product's **request policy** decides what happens next: automatic approval for eligible
   requesters, or approval by the product's approvers. Requesters can never approve their own
   request.
4. Approvers decide in the workspace or with one click in Slack, Teams or email. Approved access is
   granted immediately as a persona grant; time-boxed grants are revoked automatically when they
   expire.

marketplace.html#service-level-objective.title: Service level objectives
marketplace.html#service-level-objective.body:
A product's owners set objectives on the share of the product's quality checks that pass, on the product's **Contracts & service levels** tab (Data quality › Data product service levels lists them all) or with `PUT /cairn/api/marketplace/slos/{id}`. An example: "99% of freshness checks pass over 28 days".

| Kind | Counts the evaluations of |
|---|---|
| `freshness` | freshness monitors |
| `volume` | volume monitors |
| `quality` | field, distribution, custom SQL and schema monitors |
| `all` | every monitor on the product's datasets |

How each SLO is measured:

- **The SLI** is the share of evaluations in the window that passed (`PASS` or `WARN`). Learning-phase evaluations don't count.
- **The error budget** is what the objective allows to fail. **Budget left** is the share of it not used yet.
- **The burn rate** is how fast the last day used the budget: 1 is exactly on budget, and above 1 the budget will run out early.

**States:**

| State | When |
|---|---|
| met | the SLI meets the objective, with budget to spare |
| at risk | less than a quarter of the budget is left, or the last day burned it more than twice as fast as it should |
| breached | the SLI is below the objective |
| no data | the product has no matching checks yet |

The notifier checks hourly. The product's owners and followers get `product.slo_changed` when an SLO becomes at risk or breached, and when it recovers.

marketplace.html#sharing-outside-the-com.title: Sharing outside the company
marketplace.html#sharing-outside-the-com.body:
A data product can be offered to other companies as a **Snowflake listing** or a **Databricks Delta Sharing share**. Cairn builds it from what the catalog already knows, so nobody types the product up twice.

On the product page, an owner or admin picks the target and enters:

- a share name,
- for Snowflake, the consumer accounts (`ORG.ACCOUNT`) and the listing terms,
- for Databricks, the recipients.

**Plan** shows exactly what would run:

- **Snowflake:** a share that grants the product's Snowflake tables, and an external listing. Its manifest carries the product's description, data contracts, refresh rate, featured tables and up to three sample queries mined from real use of those tables.
- **Databricks:** a share with the product's Databricks tables and their descriptions, plus grants to recipients.

Tables on other platforms are listed as skipped. **Publish** runs the statements through a named warehouse connection, the same ones tag sync uses. With no connection, it records that you ran them yourself. Snowflake listings are created unpublished (`PUBLISH = FALSE`): review the listing in Snowflake before you release it.

**Kept in sync:** Cairn keeps a fingerprint of what it published. When the product changes (a table added or removed, a description, a contract), the owners get a notification. The publication then shows as out of date until it is published again. Republishing adds and removes tables to match, and replaces the listing's manifest (`ALTER LISTING`).

remote-agents.html#collectors-remote-age.title: Collectors (remote agents)
remote-agents.html#collectors-remote-age.body:
Collectors ingest metadata from networks Cairn cannot reach, such as a private VPC or an
on-premises data centre. They were called *remote agents* before; the UI calls them collectors (Ingestion ›
Collectors) so that *agent* means only AI agents. Nothing else changed: the API keeps its `/agents` paths (also
answered at `/collectors`), the Helm chart is still `cairn-remote-agent` (its `collector:` values block is read as
well as `agent:`), and the command is `cairn collectors run` (`cairn agent run` still works and says the new name).
Below, *agent* means a collector.

* **Outbound only.** The agent connects out to the Cairn gateway; nothing connects in.
* **Secrets stay local.** Database passwords and keys are resolved inside the agent's network and
  never sent to Cairn. Recipes with inline secrets are rejected.
* **Signed and encrypted.** Every batch is signed by the agent and end-to-end encrypted, and the
  gateway only accepts the platforms and metadata types allowed for the agent's pool.

The protocol's threat model and what the gateway refuses from an agent are on
[Remote agent security](/docs/agent-security.html).

## Set up a pool

Everything below can be done in **Workspace settings → Remote agents** (shown to people with the
Manage Ingestion privilege), or through the API.

1. Create a pool and its allowlist (**New pool**, or `POST /cairn/api/agents/pools`).

remote-agents.html#set-up-a-pool.title: Set up a pool
remote-agents.html#set-up-a-pool.body:
Everything below can be done in **Workspace settings → Remote agents** (shown to people with the
Manage Ingestion privilege), or through the API.

1. Create a pool and its allowlist (**New pool**, or `POST /cairn/api/agents/pools`).
2. Mint a one-time enrolment token (**Enrollment token** on the pool, or
   `POST /cairn/api/agents/pools/{pool}/enrollment-tokens`). The dialog shows the token once, with
   the `docker run` and Helm commands to start an agent with it.
3. Install the agent in the private network with that token (Helm chart `cairn-remote-agent`, or
   the `cairn/remote-agent` container).
4. In **Ingestion › Metadata sources**, add a source and choose the pool under **Runs on**. **Test connection**
   runs on the pool's agents. Runs are picked up by the agents in that pool, and their status,
   numbers and logs appear with the source.
